claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion under cyclic mechanical loading is governed by in situ formation and dynamic restructuring of a nanoscale passivation film.
Cyclic mechanical strain induces surface restructuring of the HEA.
Strain-induced surface restructuring heals microscale surface damage.
Mechanical strain enhances the formation and stability of an oxide or passivating film.
A stable passive film improves resistance to corrosive attack.
An oxide or passivating surface film can reduce wear damage.
Dynamic adaptation of the passivation film synergistically improves overall wear-corrosion durability.
Relative to static exposure or a matched baseline, cyclic loading will produce a denser passivation film.
Relative to static exposure or a matched baseline, cyclic loading will produce a more uniform passivation film.
The cyclically loaded alloy will have a lower wear rate than the baseline.
The cyclically loaded alloy will have a lower corrosion current density than the baseline.
The protective film and its restructuring can be observed directly by in situ high-resolution TEM or electrochemical AFM.
Zr or Mo are key alloying elements that promote the passivation behavior needed for dynamic restructuring.
Zr addition can improve wear resistance through formation of a lubricating oxide film.
Boron microalloying can stabilize a passive film and improve corrosion resistance in an AlCoCrFeNiMoTi-based HEA coating.
The predicted benefit should hold when cyclic loading is sufficient to drive restructuring and corrosion is slow enough to permit passivation-film formation.
The predicted benefit may fail under quasi-static loading or when corrosion is too rapid for film healing.
Similar film characteristics and wear-corrosion behavior under cyclic and static conditions would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: The prediction calls for lower wear under cyclic loading than under a static control, but a static specimen does not receive the same wear-producing mechanical exposure. Thus the stated control is not a matched baseline for the wear component, even though it is described as one.
